prose.title: Bear Dunn Asked for a Forecast. It Came Back With His Name on Top.
prose.dek: The bot's preseason forecast puts Bear Dunn's C-Town Chivalry on top, the defending champion close behind and Matt Gerardi's Gride at the bottom -- and between them, an order one good October could rearrange. The summer cost {{f.league.auction_spend}} and left {{f.league.cap_room}} in the whole league to change any of it.

paragraphs: Bear Dunn asked for this. In the middle of August, in the chat where these twelve argue all year, he wanted to know whether the bot could hand the league a preseason forecast. It can, and it likes him better than anybody else in the room: C-Town Chivalry first, {{f.team.0009.sim_p_title}} to win the whole thing.

The rest of the board is less obliging. Brian Cutting's Pure Greatness, the defending champion, is second. Shawn Blake is third, a hair ahead of Eric Martel, who gets Josh Jacobs back from his suspension in week three. Then it flattens out: Keith Creelman, Josh Martel, Derrick Whitman and Eric Mannila are stacked between {{f.team.0008.sim_exp_allplay}} and {{f.team.0011.sim_exp_allplay}}, close enough that one good October reshuffles all four. Brian Cross, Chris Klingenberg and Ryan Bousquet trail, and Gerardi's Gride sits by itself at the bottom, {{f.team.0003.sim_p_playoffs}} to make the playoffs.

Don't be fooled by how close the averages look. Average a team's big years with its bad ones and everybody drifts toward the middle, but real seasons never finish that bunched up. In the {{f.league.seasons_measured}} seasons this league has played, the all-play leader has averaged {{f.league.shape_first_real}} of his all-play games and the last-place team {{f.league.shape_last_real}}.

C-Town is first in the league on offense and first on defense, and that is the whole case for Dunn. Below him it gets strange. Blake bought Josh Allen at the auction and starts the best quarterback in the league. Eric Martel traded Jalen Hurts away in April, never replaced him, and starts the worst -- throwing to the best receivers and the best tight end in the league. Cross has the best defensive line and the best linebackers and still sits {{f.team.0006.power_rank|ord}}, because the offense around Hurts is thin: his receivers and his flexes both rank eleventh. And Gride is in the league's top half at exactly one spot: receiver.

Mannila is the one that looks wrong. He starts the third-most valuable offense in the league, and the forecast has him {{f.team.0011.power_rank|ord}}. Value is what his players would fetch on the redraft market; the forecast runs on MFL's weekly projections instead, and MFL is cooler than the market on CeeDee Lamb, Malik Nabers and Tucker Kraft. In the weekly points the forecast runs on, the table below, his offense is seventh, his defense is level with CBP's for the league's worst and his kicker and punter together rank tenth; the bottom four defenses there are separated by a fraction of a point. Nine of the eighteen slots a team starts are defenders, a kicker and a punter. Nobody wins a league there -- the gap from the best defense to the worst is a fraction of the gap on offense -- but a team can give away a point or two a week at nine positions at once, and those are the easiest points in the league to get back.

paragraphs: Eric Martel made the one spring trade that changed a contender. In April he sent Jalen Hurts and blind-bid money to Cross for The Long Haulers' 2027 first and second. Then he spent his own first- and second-round picks for next year on two running backs, Kenneth Walker from Creelman and David Montgomery from L.A. Looks, and restructured Walker and Ja'Marr Chase to make room. The Hurts trade is why his quarterbacks now rank last in the league.

April is where you see who was getting his money's worth. A table in the auction section below sets each owner's slice of the league's payroll against his slice of the league's starting-offense value. Payroll includes defenders and the value count does not, so a team that spent on defense looks a little worse there than it really is. Blake held a small slice of the salary and a much bigger slice of the value. Cutting and Dunn paid above-average payrolls and still held more value than they paid for. Josh Martel and Cross carried the two biggest payrolls and were paying for more than they were starting. Creelman had almost no salary and almost no team -- which turned out to be a plan, not a problem: nobody spent more at the auction.

Eric Martel opened the league's first Owner Divisional Draft by taking Cross, and in this draft that was not a compliment. The owners had voted in May to pick their own divisions: four captains, two rounds, a snake, run on rookie draft night before a single rookie was taken. The bot spelled out the logic the next morning: getting picked first means your captain thinks you are the weakest team on the board.
Bousquet welcomed Cross to the honor by telling him it was going to be a long haul. Cross, whose team is called The Long Haulers, said he had at least chosen the right name when he joined.
Two picks stand out. Dunn's first pick, {{f.league.div_draft_pick_0012|ord}} overall, was the Hawks, exactly as he had promised in January, four months before there was a draft to promise it about.

And the defending champion went last. Pure Greatness was still on the board at the {{f.league.div_draft_pick_0004|ord}} and final pick, which put it in Eric Martel's division and the last two champions in the same one. Martel had seen it coming in May, while the owners were still voting on the rule.

After the division draft came the rookie draft, and the trading ran right alongside the picks. Most of the {{f.league.rookie_picks}} picks were made that night and the last two the next morning. Eric Martel moved up twice. Creelman traded three times and spent one of the picks he got on Sonny Styles less than a minute after he got it. That pick had gone from CBP to L.A. Looks, back to CBP, to Sex Manther, to The Long Haulers and then to Gride, which held it for about an hour before sending it to Creelman.

Most of the tags did not stick. Two were trade chips: Bousquet tagged Amon-Ra St. Brown and traded him to Gride in July, and Gride tagged Travis Etienne and sent him to Creelman three days later, on draft night. Three were simply let go. Dunn tagged George Pickens in May and released him on lock day with no penalty. Blake cut the tag on Jacoby Brissett in July, and Creelman bought Brissett at the auction for less. Josh Martel released Christian McCaffrey in July, and Dunn bought him at the auction for barely more than the tag had cost. The tags that stuck: Kamren Curl, Myles Garrett, Javonte Williams and Trevor Lawrence.

paragraphs: Josh Allen went to Blake for {{f.league.faa_top_price}}, the priciest player of the summer, after fifteen bids, and the last man Blake had to outbid was Creelman. Blake's was not the biggest bill, though. Creelman spent more than any owner in the league and walked out with Dak Prescott, Saquon Barkley and Kyler Murray. Whitman spent nearly as much and bought an entire backfield, Tony Pollard included -- the same Tony Pollard that C-Town had cut on lock day to make room.

Across the Free Agent Auction and the smaller Expired Rookie Auction the twelve bought {{f.league.auction_lots}} players for {{f.league.auction_spend}}, and almost all of it, {{f.league.faa_spend}}, went at the Free Agent Auction. Even the punters had a bidding war: Blake pushed up the price on Ryan Eckley before Josh Martel took him. Thirteen days did nearly the whole year's work. Whatever a roster looked like at the lock in late July, it looked like a football team by the close in early August.

Mostly, the money did not go where the talent already was. From April to now the biggest gain belongs to Creelman, who came in with the smallest payroll in the league, and the next biggest to Whitman, who came in with the fewest players. Dunn, who already held one of the best rosters, took the third. Cutting and Mannila, sitting on two of the other best lineups, spent about as little as anybody and finished the summer where they started.

The table below tells the rest. Payroll is now nearly level: every owner carries close to a twelfth of the league's salary. Talent is not. Dunn holds a far bigger slice of the league's lineup value than of its payroll, Cutting a clearly bigger one, and Mannila, who spent less at the auction than anyone, a somewhat bigger one. The Hawks, L.A. Looks and Gride each carry about a twelfth of the league's salary and get back only about two thirds as much talent as that pays for. The league bought itself level on money and stayed unequal on players.

Defense was where the money was not. Only Cross and Eric Martel put a serious share of their budget into defenders, and it worked: The Long Haulers start the best defensive line and the best linebackers in the league. Everybody else bought offense. Everybody else was probably right.

paragraphs: Creelman made fourteen waiver pickups before week one, more than any owner in the league, most of them one-for-one swaps at the very back of his roster. One was Trey Benson, whom he had cut in July and claimed back less than three weeks later. Josh Martel had a view on all that activity.

If you want cheap points, they are on defense. The wire holds none of the league's best at any offensive position -- offense is bought in July or traded for, and that is the end of it. But {{f.league.free_db}} of the twelve best projected defensive backs are sitting there right now, along with {{f.league.free_kickers}} of the twelve best kickers and {{f.league.free_punters}} of the twelve best punters, including the best-projected punter in the league. They cost a waiver claim.

Otherwise, not much has moved. Between the close of the auction and week one the league made {{f.league.pickups}} pickups and three trades, and the twelve starting lineups look about the way the auction left them. There is not much money to change that: {{f.league.cap_committed}} is on the books and {{f.league.cap_room}} of room is left in the entire league. Whitman has none and Creelman barely any. The most room belongs to the Hawks and Gride, who also have the most holes to fill.

The forecast sits every player MFL lists as out, for as long as he is expected to miss. It also sits two players MFL had not listed yet, both hurt in the opener: Bousquet's Sam Darnold for week two and Cross's A.J. Brown for weeks two through four. C-Town opens without Brock Bowers, whose knee needed a trimmed meniscus. Eric Martel thought the report made surgery sound like a haircut.

As for week one itself: four NFL teams had finished when this was put together. The owners whose players happen to have played already look better than the owners whose players have not, and that is the entire content of it. Blake spent Thursday night defending George Kittle, and Cutting was not impressed. Klingenberg, meanwhile, is crediting Blake with breaking injury news faster than Schefter.

paragraphs: The owners drew these divisions themselves and are stuck with them through 2028, so it matters which one came out strongest. The forecast says Outlast PG Time: Pure Greatness, HammerTime and The Long Haulers average {{f.league.div_outlastpgtime_allplay}} in projected all-play, carry the best combined title odds in the league at {{f.league.div_outlastpgtime_title}}, and spent less at the auction than any other division. Cross pitched a name for it on draft night and again in June -- two recent champions and a problem, with himself as the problem. The name that stuck was Outlast PG Time. The forecast kept his joke anyway: the champions are second and fourth in the league, and Cross is {{f.team.0006.power_rank|ord}}. Eric Martel calls himself and Pure Greatness a coin flip for the division; the forecast gives Cutting the edge, {{f.team.0004.sim_p_division}} to {{f.team.0005.sim_p_division}}.

DOG POUND 4 LIFE is a hair behind at {{f.league.div_dogpound4life_allplay}}. Its combined title odds are {{f.league.div_dogpound4life_title}}, and Dunn accounts for about two thirds of that by himself, with Mannila and Klingenberg well behind. It is the division with the best team in it and not the best three.

Maddie Mondays and LEGION OF BOOM finish level, at {{f.league.div_maddiemondays_allplay}} and {{f.league.div_legionofboom_allplay}}, and got there in opposite ways. Maddie Mondays is the tightest division in the league and spent the most at the auction: Creelman and Josh Martel are separated by less than a point of all-play, with Bousquet the one team trailing. LEGION OF BOOM is the widest: Blake third in the league, Gerardi twelfth, Whitman in between. Blake can win it; Gride is what drags it down.

None of this is a promise. Replayed on the last five seasons, the forecast called the order nearly right in the first two and only loosely in the three since, and this year's rosters are bunched closer than in any of them. Read it as odds: Gride finishes in the top three in {{f.team.0003.sim_p_top3}} of the {{f.league.sim_runs}} simulated seasons, and C-Town finishes last in {{f.team.0009.sim_p_last}}. These divisions are locked for three seasons, and year one starts now.

paragraphs: This is how the forecast works, and how it would have done. The projections are MFL's own: projected points for every player in every week, under this league's scoring.

Each simulated week the model starts every team's best lineup from those projections. Players MFL lists as out sit for the weeks they are expected to miss, and so do two whose injuries had been reported but not yet listed. At every position a waiver-level player is available to every team, and he starts wherever he projects better than what the team has, because an owner with a hole or a weak spot picks somebody up. The model keeps only {{f.league.sim_regress}} of each team's projected edge over the league, because preseason favorites fall back toward the pack more often than they pull away. Then it adds luck twice: once for the whole season, since some teams simply are better or worse than their projections, and once every week. It plays the real schedule, crowns the division winners, runs the six-team bracket, and does all of that {{f.league.sim_runs}} times.

The fair test of a forecast is whether it would have worked before. A simpler version of the same model was replayed on 2021 through 2025. It used each player's week-one projection for the whole season, with no injury hold-outs, because MFL's archived projections for later weeks were made during the season and already knew each week's injury news, which a preseason forecast could not have. Across those {{f.league.bt_team_seasons}} team-seasons its projections accounted for {{f.league.bt_r2}} of the variation in final all-play: it saw a real part of what was coming and missed more than half of it. Its typical miss was {{f.league.bt_rmse}} points of all-play, against {{f.league.bt_rmse_500}} if you simply called every team a coin flip.

The order is the weak part. It had 2021 and 2022 nearly right, scoring {{f.league.bt_rho_2021}} and {{f.league.bt_rho_2022}} on a scale where one is the exact order and zero is no relation at all. The last three came in at {{f.league.bt_rho_2023}}, {{f.league.bt_rho_2024}} and {{f.league.bt_rho_2025}}: only loosely right. Last season it had Sex Manther dead last, and Josh Martel finished runner-up.

Its settings were tuned on those same seasons, so read what follows as a check, not proof. Kept whole, the projected gaps between teams came out too big: the real gaps were only about two thirds of them. Trimmed to {{f.league.sim_regress}}, the projected gaps matched the real ones almost exactly and the typical miss was at its smallest. The playoff odds held up: teams it gave long odds rarely made it, and teams it gave strong odds usually did. And {{f.league.bt_inside_band}} of the {{f.league.bt_team_seasons}} teams finished inside their own big-year to bad-year range, though the luck in the model was sized to those seasons, so the ranges were always likely to fit.

This year is harder to call than any season it was tested on. The typical team projects {{f.league.bt_sd_now_pre}} all-play points from the league average on week-one projections, against at least {{f.league.bt_sd_low_pre}} in every tested season, and {{f.league.bt_sd_now}} on the projections this forecast uses, against at least {{f.league.bt_sd_low_weekly}}. To spread the finish out like a real season, the model has to add more luck: a team's whole season can run about {{f.league.sim_shock}} fantasy points a week above or below its projection, more than any tested year needed (the most was {{f.league.bt_shock_high_weekly}}). More of this forecast is luck and less of it is rosters.

What it cannot do. It sees nothing that happens after it runs: no trades, no pickups beyond its waiver stand-ins, no new injuries. It starts the best lineup every week, which owners do not. It uses one projection source, and MFL disagrees with the market on some stars. And it grades rosters, not the men who run them.
